title: About This Channel
principle: Explain design ideas simply, in short bite-sized units
why: He keeps things simple so people without development experience can follow, and keeps each video to 2-5 minutes because the longer he talks, the harder it is to retain everything.
how: When briefing or teaching, spell out even 'common knowledge' concepts and split topics into short units.
anti_pattern: Long, technical explanations that assume expert knowledge.
quote: In fact, I think keeping things simple is for the best.

title: Presentations Are All About Speed!
principle: Keep presentations fast: go straight to the core idea
why: Creators must communicate their ideas, and his secret to doing it well is speed: trimming the fat and getting right to the heart of the topic.
how: Cut anything not serving the core idea, drop justifications and alternatives, and use simple graphics.
anti_pattern: Long preambles, justifications and lists of alternatives.
quote: Keep those presentations speedy. Trim the fat, and get right to the heart of your topic. Forget justifications or alternatives.

title: Presentations Are All About Speed!
principle: Fill your time, but never let the pace stall
why: A presentation doesn't have to be short; what matters most is keeping things moving and making the most of the time you have.
how: Rehearse for pace rather than brevity, and keep each part moving to the next.
anti_pattern: Confusing speed with cutting the presentation short.
quote: And remember, it doesn't have to be short. Just keep things moving and make the most of the time you have.

title: Assigning Animations
principle: Show key poses with photographs of a posed figure
why: Text alone isn't enough for crucial poses like idles, movement and attacks; photographed figure poses make it clear what moves should look like.
how: Pose a figure, photograph it, cut out the shape, adjust contrast and add it to the spec sheet; add source-game screenshots when relevant and use text only for non-humanoid characters.
example: Super Smash Bros. spec sheets, 70-80 pages of images per fighter on average.
quote: Take your figure. Photograph it. Cut out the shape. Adjust the contrast.

title: Assigning Animations
principle: Give animation direction with all animators present
why: Sharing practical knowledge and pointers with everyone helps the team avoid repeating the same missteps and improves everyone's skills together.
how: Hold feedback sessions with the whole animation team rather than one-on-one.
anti_pattern: Feedback given privately that others never hear.
quote: Whenever I give directions about animation, I make sure all my animators are present.

title: Try Telling That to the Player
principle: Put player experience ahead of development convenience in specs
why: Design documents often come back prioritizing the developers' jobs; sometimes that's a sensible efficiency compromise, but players only care whether the game is good and won't cut you slack.
how: Flag every spec decision made for convenience and keep it only if players won't suffer for it.
anti_pattern: Specs that prioritize ease of development over the player.
example: A designer's design document.
quote: Players aren't concerned about why developers do what they do. They only care if a game is good or not.

title: Try Telling That to the Player
principle: Balance ideal and feasible together with your programmers
why: This isn't just a design issue; you need to strike a balance between what's ideal and what's technologically feasible.
how: Bring programmers into discussions about compromises early to find feasible ways to keep the player experience.
quote: Talk to your programmers, too. In the end, you'll need to strike a balance between what's ideal and what's technologically feasible.

title: Spec Changes
principle: Report problems the moment you spot them, with everything you know.
why: Players can't fix what's wrong but the team can, and the sooner problems are raised, the less time is wasted.
how: Make it a team rule that anyone tells the lead right away and shares all their information without debating how to phrase it.
anti_pattern: Saying "I knew that was wrong!" after the fact.
quote: As soon as you spot an issue, you have to tell someone right away.

title: Spec Changes
principle: Put every option on the table, then decide quickly.
why: Long deliberation wastes time, but decisions need accurate information, and collective knowledge beats any one person's.
how: Gather all known facts and options, pick the one that works short- and long-term, and decide immediately.
anti_pattern: Digging in your heels on an idea that isn't working.
quote: The moment a problem crops up, I make a decision immediately rather than spending time on it.

title: Emphasize Objects with Collision
principle: Make sure artists understand each asset's role in gameplay.
why: An artist's job isn't just producing artwork; the art has to suit its function in the game.
how: Brief artists on which elements are collidable, and review their art in gameplay context rather than as standalone pictures.
anti_pattern: Treating art as standalone pieces.
quote: An artist's job isn't just producing artwork and calling it a day— understand your art's role in the game and make what's appropriate!

title: Breaking Down Attack Animations
principle: Spec attacks by standby pose, attack pose, start frame and total frames.
why: The lead-in and follow-through fit between those markers, so these four facts give animators a good starting point.
how: In every animation request, list the standby pose, the attack key pose, the frame the hit starts, and total frames until cancelable.
quote: The standby pose. The attack pose. The attack start frame. and the total frames— or the time until the attack can be canceled.

title: Writing Game Proposals
principle: Talk around your slides; never read them aloud.
why: Slides that are a wall of text read out loud are annoying, and people just read ahead.
how: Keep slide text minimal and say a little about each slide in your own words.
anti_pattern: Reading a wall of text straight off the page.
quote: It can be pretty annoying when a slide is just a wall of text the presenter reads out loud.

title: Sharing Info Within a Team
principle: Keep a daily report page the whole team can read and comment on.
why: On large games people lose sight of what they're making, and working without the larger picture is stressful.
how: Post progress, news and your thoughts on the project every day, like a development newspaper, with a comment field for the team.
example: Sakurai's Daily Report.
quote: But working like that—without a clear vision of the larger picture—is stressful, in my opinion.

title: Sharing Info Within a Team
principle: Share one in-progress screenshot with the team every day.
why: It shows everyone where the game stands, including content unfit for the public, and writing captions in the comments helps the team unwind.
how: Attach a daily screenshot to the report page and invite comments and captions.
example: Screenshot of the Day, later repurposed for his daily screens on Twitter.
quote: The team really enjoyed coming up with captions for these in the comments, so it was a nice way to unwind.

title: Sharing Info Within a Team
principle: Hold cross-discipline progress presentations every few months.
why: Everyone gets a broader view of the project instead of feeling like mere cogs, plus motivation and a sense of accomplishment.
how: Have each team (graphics, sound, animation, VFX, UI) present its work to everyone, despite scheduling and venue hassles.
anti_pattern: Skipping them because they're a hassle to organize.
example: Project Presentations on Sakurai's teams.
quote: By having the teams present their progress, everyone gets a broader view of the project instead of feeling like mere cogs in a machine.

title: Distinguishing Between Major and Minor Elements
principle: Cut detail nobody will see, but allow harmless playfulness.
why: A bit of playfulness makes the game better if it meets deadlines and doesn't hurt performance, but invisible details waste resources.
how: Approve small extras that don't affect schedule or frame rate; ask the team to tone down ones no player will ever notice.
anti_pattern: Animating details truly nobody will see.
example: Turning car tires in the backdrop of Inkling's stage.
quote: It was something truly nobody would see.

title: Making Your Game Easy to Tune
principle: Let more team members adjust parameters easily.
why: When more people can adjust values, trial and error is easy and more values get tuned more deeply; early on, Sakurai wrote every parameter himself.
how: Store parameters in an accessible format so designers beyond the lead can tune them.
anti_pattern: A single person as the only one who can change values.
example: Smash Bros. for Wii U/3DS onward.
quote: our parameters are maintained in a way that lets more people adjust them easily

title: Jobs in Game Development
principle: Share objectives and goals with every role on the team
why: Directors, planners, programmers, artists, sound, UI, tech ops, managers and testers must work in tandem, and nothing gets done without mutual understanding.
how: Organize subteams (e.g. characters, stages) that mix professions, keep the director involved in each, and make the project's goals visible to everyone, not only to leads.
example: The Smash Bros. Ultimate fighter team: planners, programmers, modelers, artists, animators, effect and sound designers
quote: Objectives and goals should be shared with everyone, so the entire team can move forward together.

title: Jobs in Game Development
principle: Have planners turn the director's ideas into programmable spec sheets
why: Spec sheets carry the detailed information about how the game should be programmed; planners also balance gameplay, manage teams and supervise testing.
how: Assign a planner role that writes design documents from the director's ideas and distributes them, and have programmers implement from those documents.
quote: In short, they turn the director's ideas into design documents and distribute them to the team.

title: Jobs in Game Development
principle: Require reproduction steps in bug reports and route each to an owner
why: Bug testers' reports only get fixed when the right team takes them over; play testers' feedback is examined by planning.
how: Have bug testers write how to reproduce each bug, have a manager assign it to the team that owns it, and choose play testers for competitive games with enough skill and perseverance.
quote: After they write up a bug report explaining how to reproduce a bug, a manager assigns it to the appropriate team, who takes over until the bug is fixed.

title: Kirby Air Ride
principle: Step in and rebuild on fresh specs when delegated core gameplay stalls
why: After a year of delegated development not a single Warp Star worked right; with new specs and existing assets the game was finished in three and a half months.
how: When core gameplay stalls, have the director return, write new specifications, and rebuild the game logic while reusing finished assets.
anti_pattern: Leaving stalled core gameplay delegated indefinitely.
example: Kirby Air Ride's rebuild at the lead programmer's request
quote: After a year of delegating the development, not even a single Warp Star worked right.

title: Don't Wait to Speak Your Mind
principle: Voice concerns immediately to people who can act on them
why: Waiting until after the project only satisfies your ego and upsets teammates; unlike players, developers can still fix things, and quick course-corrections make goals easier to reach.
how: Raise the issue as soon as you notice it and make it visible to the people who can do something about it.
anti_pattern: Hiding your feelings and revealing them after the project ends.
quote: Whether or not your opinion would have changed things, if you wait, it's too late!

title: Don't Wait to Speak Your Mind
principle: Pair every problem you raise with a proposed solution
why: It fosters a constructive dev environment, and your suggestion might end up helping many players; if the team keeps things as they are, hearing their reasons helps you accept it.
how: Present the complaint and at least one possible fix together, then listen to the team's reasons if they decide otherwise.
anti_pattern: Only saying "This isn't good."
quote: Make the problem and the potential solution a set package.

title: Don't Wait to Speak Your Mind
principle: Give the whole team an open opinion board
why: It's important to hear everyone's opinions, and some people won't speak up otherwise.
how: Create a board where any team member can write about how development is going; have the director reply or forward items to the right team.
anti_pattern: Letting posts get lost in the flow without a response.
example: Opinion boards on Sakurai's recent projects
quote: On recent projects of mine, I've set up "opinion boards," where team members are free to write their opinions on how development is going.

title: Don't Wait to Speak Your Mind
principle: Listen flexibly and decide quickly when receiving opinions
why: A broader viewpoint and deeper understanding help you reach solutions quickly, and quick course corrections help the project.
how: Weigh the pros and cons of each opinion promptly and stay open to changing course.
quote: And if you're on the listening end of these opinions, try to be flexible.

title: Sora's Work-From-Home Strategies
principle: Survey the team early after a big workflow change
why: It was a first attempt and many issues cropped up; the survey revealed problems many people shared (desks, reference monitors, internet, playtesting, social contact).
how: Shortly after switching to remote work, ask everyone what's working and what isn't, then fix the common issues first.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate's switch to remote work in April 2020
quote: A little after we started working remotely, I sent out a survey to everyone on the team and asked for their thoughts on how it was going.

title: Sora's Work-From-Home Strategies
principle: Solve remote-work problems fast by buying equipment centrally
why: Many issues could be solved with supplies, a missing desk and chair would cause health problems, and per-company procedures and approvals on a mixed team would eat time.
how: Let anyone send a product link; one budget orders it, ships it to their home, and they keep it.
anti_pattern: Leaving each partner company to run its own purchasing and approvals.
example: Sora Ltd.'s supplementary budget for the Smash Bros. Ultimate team
quote: To solve the problem as quickly as possible, I had Sora foot the bill for everyone.

title: Sora's Work-From-Home Strategies
principle: Plan for a productivity drop and stay flexible
why: In Sakurai's estimation, productivity fell by about 30%, and pandemic delays are a real occurrence.
how: Account for reduced output in remote schedules, move rituals like daily test matches online, and look for new ways forward.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate DLC development
quote: But just like with every situation, you need to be as flexible as you can, and ready to find a new way forward.

title: Directors Need to Be Unique
principle: Pair a unique vision with balance and clear communication
why: Quirkiness helps, but directors also need a good sense of balance and the skill to communicate their creative ideas; he can hardly think of directors who can't converse.
how: Practice explaining your ideas to teammates until they can restate them accurately.
anti_pattern: Being so idiosyncratic that the team can't follow your ideas.
quote: They should probably be skilled at communicating their creative ideas, too.

title: Mastering Up
principle: Show appreciation to the staff when you master up
why: Finishing usually involves tough decisions and cut content, so the moment can feel wounding, which makes you want to thank those who made it through.
how: At master-up, explicitly recognize and thank the team, whatever state the project ended in.
quote: Still, it makes you want to show appreciation for the staff that made it through that hardship with you.

title: Ten People Can Produce Seven People's Work
principle: Budget for management: ten people yield about seven people's work
why: Running a team takes management time: workloads, outside communication and creative supervision all pull people away from production.
how: Plan schedules assuming roughly 70% effective output from headcount, with more overhead as the team grows, and name who owns each management role.
anti_pattern: Planning as if headcount equals output.
quote: It depends on the situation, of course, but 10 people can generally produce seven people's worth of work.

title: Ten People Can Produce Seven People's Work
principle: Expect to lose a skilled creator's output when they lead
why: Skilled workers moving into leadership can't replicate their output at scale; they become the brains who set direction and maintain quality.
how: When promoting a strong creator to lead, backfill their production work in the schedule.
anti_pattern: Expecting new leads to keep their full individual output.
quote: When an experienced creative eye shifts over to the management side, that obviously means you lose the share of work they would have produced.

title: Ten People Can Produce Seven People's Work
principle: Hold regular meetings where each subteam presents its finished work
why: It lets everyone see the whole project, builds presentation skills and deepens awareness that they are making something for others.
how: Schedule a recurring showcase where each subteam, such as the character team, presents what it finished that period.
quote: To help team members get a top-down view of the whole project, I recommend holding meetings where each subteam presents the fruits of their labor.

title: Supervising Art Through Retouches
principle: Give art feedback with a quick retouch instead of words
why: Palette and contrast changes are hard to explain verbally, and a retouch taking about five to ten minutes is more efficient than explaining.
how: Spend 5-10 minutes on a rough paintover of the artist's piece and send it side by side with the original.
anti_pattern: Trying to retouch every asset, or long verbal descriptions of visual changes.
example: Retouched backgrounds for a Spirits exploration cave, the Marx boss fight and a World of Light path.
quote: When supervising a game's graphics, there's no better way to explain what you want than by just showing it.

title: Supervising Art Through Retouches
principle: Treat retouches as direction and let artists execute
why: Supervision is charting the creative course; reaching release quality takes serious work by the artist, and first-try approvals are best for everyone.
how: Label retouches as examples and leave final execution to the artist.
anti_pattern: Treating the director's retouch as final art.
quote: In the end, supervision is really just charting the creative course.

title: Using Tickets to Manage Tasks
principle: Turn every task into a ticket with one clear owner
why: Tickets passed between team members through a server tool make it clear who is responsible for what, so status is easy to confirm and nothing slips through the cracks.
how: Split one character into tickets for spec/doc, model and rig, animation, programming, VFX, SFX and balancing, each assigned to a leader or team member.
anti_pattern: Work that lives only in conversation, with no owner or status.
example: Making one game character: every production step becomes a ticket passed from team to team.
quote: Manage those tasks, and make it crystal clear what needs to happen.

title: Using Tickets to Manage Tasks
principle: Give every ticket a status and a deadline a lead tracks
why: Statuses like in progress, complete, on hold and rescinded make it easy to judge how things are going, and a leader tracking deadlines can head off delays.
how: Require a status field and due date on each ticket and have leads review open tickets regularly.

title: Using Tickets to Manage Tasks
principle: Avoid lining up dependent tasks so directly back-to-back
why: Downstream jobs depend on upstream ones (the animator can't work until the model is ready), and when work runs late the next person ends up starting early with whatever they have.
how: Let dependent job types share a ticket and leave scheduling slack between upstream and downstream work.
anti_pattern: Forcing downstream staff to start on unfinished upstream work.
example: Animation waiting on the character model.
quote: it's better to avoid lining tasks up so directly when possible.

title: Using Tickets to Manage Tasks
principle: Route bug reports through tickets via section leaders
why: Testers confirm the bug and write the report inside the ticket, and the section leader distributes it to the right people; anyone can reassign it if it reached the wrong person or needs more eyes.
how: Have testers file confirmed bugs as tickets, route them through leads, and allow free reassignment.
example: Bug testers receiving, confirming and returning tickets.

title: Don't Rely on a "Plan B"
principle: Resolve spec problems together with the team after proposing
why: The proposal-writer should start with the ideal, field plenty of suggestions with an open mind, and address problems as a team, even if that ends at Plan B.
how: Circulate the proposal, gather team feedback, and revisit alternatives only when real problems arise.
quote: If problems arise, you can then address them as a team.

title: Canceled Games
principle: Make everyone aware of what it takes to finish the game
why: The more each team member knows what's needed to finish, the better the odds of seeing it through; finishing assignments alone doesn't guarantee a finished product.
how: Share a visible picture of everything remaining to ship, not just per-person task lists, and work through it together.
anti_pattern: Assuming the game will ship just because everyone completes their assigned tasks.
quote: At the very least, you shouldn't assume that you'll end up with a finished product just because everyone completes what they're assigned.

title: Explain Ideas to Everyone at Once
principle: Give feedback to every involved discipline at the same time
why: On Kid Icarus: Uprising, instructions relayed through a planner to programmers sometimes came back as the polar opposite of what he wanted.
how: Have planners, programmers, modelers, animators, VFX, sound and their leads all attend feedback sessions, with the build on a big monitor and a mic.
anti_pattern: Relaying a director's intent through a chain of people.
example: Super Smash Bros.: Inkling's special-move spec supervision.
quote: Namely, whenever I gave instructions or feedback, all relevant team members were required to attend and listen.

title: Explain Ideas to Everyone at Once
principle: Let people see the feedback others receive
why: When team members see everyone's feedback, not just their own, they all learn and grow, and visibility improves on large projects.
how: Hold group review sessions per discipline and let anyone sit in on feedback, even from other teams.
example: Group review sessions for fighter modelers, artists, stage modelers and animators.
quote: By having team members see the feedback everyone was getting—not just their own— they could all learn and grow.

title: Explain Ideas to Everyone at Once
principle: Keep group feedback sessions speedy
why: Extra meetings can look wasteful, and the system only works if they stay quick.
how: Run tight sessions: show the screen, explain with a mic, then take questions at the end.
anti_pattern: Letting large group meetings drag on.
quote: It does require you to keep those meetings speedy for it to work, but I really do recommend it.

title: Daily Report Suggestions
principle: Post a daily internal report with a screenshot and 3-5 topics
why: Team-wide emails often go unread, but a page with something new every day is one people keep up with on their own, making it a more reliable channel.
how: Each workday, post a current screenshot plus news, your work, checklists and issues to fix, with comments enabled; use it for key announcements.
anti_pattern: Relying on mass email for important information.
example: Smash Bros. Brawl onward; a Sephiroth reveal via the report crashed the server.
quote: However, the Daily Report offers something new every day— so most people take it upon themselves to keep up with it

title: Daily Report Suggestions
principle: Let the team know you personally, especially as an outside director
why: Taking direction from an unknown outsider doesn't feel good; reading his reports meant Sakurai was no longer a total stranger.
how: Mix non-work topics into your reports (games you played, current events, your thoughts) and vary them daily.
example: Sakurai joining existing teams as a freelance director.

title: Daily Report Suggestions
principle: Show everyone the whole game's progress every day
why: On big teams each person's work is one small part, and they can lose sight of the bigger picture without seeing what others make.
how: Share a daily screenshot of the current build and invite members to post what they finished that day.
example: Screenshot of the Day, later shared publicly on Twitter.

title: Daily Report Suggestions
principle: Give the team an easy channel for suggestions and requests
why: Sakurai set up an "opinions board" when joining teams and found it effective for gathering input.
how: Create a simple board where anyone can submit suggestions and requests at any time.

title: Arranging Music
principle: Route music feedback through someone with musical vocabulary
why: Sakurai may know how he wants something but lack the musical language to express it, so passing feedback through the sound director gets the best results.
how: Run several review rounds covering tempo, intonation, transcription accuracy and direction, delivered via your sound director.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate's sound director.

title: Arranging Music
principle: Match each piece to a composer's attachment or strengths
why: It's best when composers arrange a piece they have an attachment to; even versatile composers have areas where they excel most.
how: Let composers choose first; when assigning, pick the piece that best suits each composer's strengths.
example: Super Smash Bros. arrangement assignments.

title: Motion Sickness in 3D Games
principle: Test camera comfort with players prone to motion sickness
why: Motion sickness varies greatly between people, so a team where nobody suffers from it will struggle to catch the problem.
how: Recruit testers who get 3D motion sickness and review camera options with them.
anti_pattern: Signing off camera comfort based on a team that never feels sick.

title: The Team Behind Super Smash Bros. Brawl
principle: Build the core team from people who love the game
why: The Game Arts core team had played so much Melee their stick ridges were worn down, and both executives and developers were excited for the project.
how: When recruiting a core team, favor people who know and are enthusiastic about the series or genre.
example: Game Arts staff for Super Smash Bros. Brawl.

title: Super Smash Bros. for 3DS / Wii U
principle: Move parameter entry off the director onto a small planner team
why: Sakurai had entered every parameter himself on earlier games despite heavy supervision, approval and marketing duties, which he says he should never have done. An efficient pipeline let planners take over.
how: Build tools and pipelines that let a few planners enter and tune data, add more play testers to judge versus balance, and keep the director supervising.
anti_pattern: The director personally inputting all parameters on top of every other duty.
example: From Smash for 3DS / Wii U, planners handled tuning. On Ultimate, Sakurai only supervised.

title: Staying Organized with Hierarchical Outlines
principle: Clean up personal idea outlines before putting them on shared servers
why: Sakurai mostly uses outlines to compile his own ideas, and design documents usually end up on a shared company server, so others will read them.
how: Do a cleanup pass on your private outline before sharing it as a design document.
anti_pattern: Posting a raw personal idea dump as the team's spec.

title: The Original Piece is Always Right
principle: When revisions contradict your feedback, check that your terms match
why: Arrangement changes on Athena kept coming back as the opposite of Sakurai's feedback because he and the musicians meant different things by "main melody."
how: When notes seem ignored, play the reference together and agree on what each term refers to before giving more feedback.
anti_pattern: Repeating the same notes louder without checking definitions.
example: Athena arrangement for Smash Bros.

title: The Majority Shouldn't Always Rule
principle: Let the person with the big picture decide, not a majority vote
why: In creative work more votes don't mean a better answer; majority choices end up the safest and most mediocre, and ideas everyone opposed in planning often turn out fun once built.
how: When the team is split, have the director make the call and explain the reasoning; build promising unpopular ideas and judge them in the game.
anti_pattern: Settling design direction by headcount.
example: Metal Gear Solid 3 — the wound treatment system had only four supporters at first
quote: Ideas decided by majority end up being the safest ideas. In other words, the most mediocre.

title: The Majority Shouldn't Always Rule
principle: Share every problem and possible solution with the decision-maker
why: Whoever holds the power must stay balanced and well informed; without transparency anyone can make the wrong call, and without reasoning direction turns into dictatorship.
how: Before major decisions, ask the team to lay out the problems and candidate solutions they see, then decide with that information.
anti_pattern: A leader barking irrational orders with paper-thin reasoning.
quote: Anyone could make the wrong call when faced with a lack of transparency.

title: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate
principle: Have the next proposal ready before the current project wraps
why: Sakurai finished Ultimate's 200-plus-page proposal the same day as Smash for's final video presentation, because staying ahead was the only way to keep the dev team together.
how: Draft the follow-up proposal, with feature lists and per-character adjustments, during the tail end of the current project.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate — proposal finished the same day Smash for's final presentation aired
quote: I had to stay ahead if I wanted to keep the dev team together.

title: Making Games as Part of a Company
principle: Don't blame a single person for a game's poor sales
why: Visuals, title, advertising, competing titles, market timing and platform all play a part, so poor sales can't truly be any one person's fault.
how: In a post-release review, look across the whole chain from visuals and title to timing and platform before drawing conclusions.
anti_pattern: Pinning a flop on one person.
quote: No single person was responsible for making and selling the game, so poor sales can't be pinned on any one person.

title: Odds and Ends of Supervising
principle: Show visual feedback with retouched images instead of describing it
why: Remote supervision runs mostly on text, but showing communicates more clearly than telling, so Sakurai retouches or draws art himself to explain each request.
how: Attach a paintover, retouched screenshot or diagram next to the original for every visual note, with one line on what to change.
anti_pattern: Text-only feedback on a visual problem.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate — retouches for Steve, Pyra/Mythra, Kazuya and event banners
quote: but since showing tends to communicate more clearly than telling, I sometimes retouch or draw art myself to explain what I mean.

title: Finish Everything Within the Day
principle: Answer every review request within the same day
why: Slow replies keep team members waiting, delaying a key member's decision can put a whole team behind, and fast replies make later review rounds easier.
how: Reply as soon as a request arrives, or right after the review you're on; never let unread requests carry over to the next day.
anti_pattern: Letting review emails accumulate, which also makes the next day more miserable.
example: Sakurai responds to every review email the same day no matter how many pile up.
quote: But no matter how many come in, and no matter how many pile up, I've always made it a point to respond to them within the same day.

title: Finish Everything Within the Day
principle: Use one fixed channel and first-come order for review requests
why: Instant messaging and ticketing systems each have drawbacks; a single predictable process keeps reviews fair and trackable.
how: Have team members email a 'Review Request' when production work is finished, handle them in arrival order, and explain any changes to everyone involved.
example: Sakurai's email-only Review Request workflow.

title: Finish Everything Within the Day
principle: Reserve a daily block with no reviews for your own work
why: Review emails arrive in erratic bursts that fragment a director's schedule, and directors have plenty of non-supervision work.
how: Pick a timeframe, such as mornings or after a set cutoff, when you stop reviewing and work only on your own tasks.
anti_pattern: Leaving yourself open for supervision all day long.

title: Staying True to Your Concept
principle: As director, keep the team oriented on the concept
why: Team members often can't grasp a new game's appeal from design docs until it exists, and unplanned elements can become core fun.
how: Repeatedly restate the concept and steer the team back toward it so their work stays usable.
anti_pattern: Expecting the design document alone to convey the fun.
example: People told Sakurai after release, 'Now I see what you were getting at.'

title: Turning Gift-Giving Into a Game
principle: Turn team giveaways into quick games instead of random handouts
why: Making games and events out of giveaways serves as an icebreaker, and everyone who has fun wins.
how: List items on a shared daily page, let interested people sign up, then pick winners by rock-paper-scissors, a match in your game, a tricky-move race or a secret rule.
anti_pattern: Handing items out at random.
example: Sakurai used the Daily Report page, Smash Bros. battles, Samurai Kirby and a secret closest-to-0-seconds rule.
quote: After all, if you're giving something away, the real winner is anyone who has fun.

title: Turning Gift-Giving Into a Game
principle: Invest in a warm relationship between director and team
why: A good director–team relationship is how game development should be, and it shows in things like the team giving the director birthday presents.
how: Share spare items and run small fun events with the team regularly.
example: Sakurai's team gave him a wide variety of birthday presents.

title: Don’t Put Decisions Off
principle: Make decisions on the spot, not later
why: Each decision sends the team down a long production path, and every minute they wait is a minute the issue stays unresolved; a quick, firm call helps more people than you'd imagine.
how: Push whoever has authority in the meeting to decide before it ends; if you're the decider, decide as soon as a team member comes to you and research immediately if needed.
anti_pattern: Saying 'I'll have to decide on this later!'
quote: When it comes to making decisions, it's best to think that "later" is too late!

title: Don’t Put Decisions Off
principle: Feed decision-makers accurate, reliable information
why: If the relevant resources aren't reliable, the decision itself won't be either.
how: When raising an issue for a decision, bring verified information so the call can be made quickly and soundly.

title: Don’t Put Decisions Off
principle: Correct wrong decisions with frequent slight adjustments
why: Decisions set the project's trajectory, so small course corrections keep it on the right path.
how: When you notice a mistake, revise the decision instead of sticking to it because it was already made.
anti_pattern: Staying the course on a known error.

title: Bug Testing Systems
principle: Test only on the latest daily build, and require reproduction steps
why: Bugs found on the wrong version aren't helpful and can cause problems, and a reproducible ticket can be tracked and assigned so nothing is overlooked.
how: Make the latest daily build mandatory for testers, and file each bug as an online ticket only once it can be reproduced.
anti_pattern: Accepting bug reports from outdated builds.
quote: To start, as a fundamental rule, we have to make sure that everyone is using the latest daily build of the game.

title: Bug Testing Systems
principle: Classify bugs by severity and route each to the discipline that owns it
why: Class S (hangs, save corruption) and Class A (progression blockers) come first, and programmers aren't always the right fixers: artists fix characters and animators fix animations.
how: Have a manager tag each ticket S, A or lower (lower ones may be waived), assign it to the right subteam or person, and rebalance anyone with too many tickets.
anti_pattern: Sending every bug to programmers by default.
quote: Programmers aren't always the right people to fix bugs, after all.

title: Bug Testing Systems
principle: Verify fixes across configurations and keep tickets as resolved
why: Every fix risks introducing new bugs and old bugs can come back, so confirmed fixes stay on record instead of being discarded.
how: Return each fixed ticket to its tester to confirm in several configurations, set it to resolved, and cross-reference or merge related tickets.
anti_pattern: Deleting tickets once they are fixed.
quote: However, the trickiest thing about bugs is that whenever you resolve one, you run the risk of introducing new bugs.

title: Final Output
principle: Give post-processing and final output a dedicated specialist
why: Sakurai expects experts who oversee post-processing to become the norm and greatly raise the overall quality of in-game visuals.
how: On high-end projects, assign one person to own post-processing and sign off on the final rendered image.
quote: I imagine any team would want to have such a specialist on board.

title: Play Testing Keeps Going
principle: Delegate balance analysis to dedicated play testers and trust them
why: Testers battle each other day in and day out and are more attuned to balance than the director, and Sakurai setting every parameter himself through Melee took all he had.
how: Staff full-time play testers, feed their opinions into tuning of every parameter, and use online and tournament results when available.
anti_pattern: A director setting every parameter alone on top of directing.
example: Brawl had only four testers; Ultimate had a much larger, more skilled team plus online data.
quote: However, the play testing team is far more attuned to that than I am, and they battle each other day in and day out, so I trust their analysis.

title: Play Testing Keeps Going
principle: As director, intervene on balance mainly to protect character individuality
why: Sakurai wants each fighter to be highly unique and player opinions to be divided, and he accepts some unfairness in isolated parts for the sake of individuality.
how: Play the build yourself regularly (he plays 30 minutes of multiplayer at lunch) and step in when a proposed change erodes a character's distinctiveness.
quote: When I do end up saying something, it's most often because a fighter's individuality is being threatened.

title: All to Destroy One Wall
principle: Give art feedback as paint-overs with specific, concrete fixes
why: Retouched images made it much clearer what Sakurai wanted than words alone, and specific notes let the team act on each problem.
how: Draw over deliveries and name exact changes: avoid perpendicular cuts, keep the X-axis flat, make spacing erratic, vary copy-pasted patterns.
anti_pattern: Vague notes like "make it look better".
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate's Mishima Dojo destructible wall went through several rounds of retouched feedback images.

title: All to Destroy One Wall
principle: Judge assets by their core purpose, not by your mental image
why: The wall only had to look like wooden boards had actually been broken; work that differs from the director's picture is fine if the quality is there.
how: State each asset's goal in one sentence and approve anything that meets it.
anti_pattern: Forcing every asset to conform to the director's personal ideal.
quote: My goal isn't to make everything in the game conform to my ideals, so I make these decisions surprisingly often.

title: All to Destroy One Wall
principle: Accept and ship an asset when repeated feedback stops converging
why: Supervision often yields a half-step when you hoped for a whole step, and big swings each round feel like changing direction; the director and artist share responsibility.
how: After several rounds without reaching the bar, put the asset in the game as-is and move on.
anti_pattern: Changing direction with every round of feedback.
quote: Whenever such cases arise... it's best to accept it and move on.

title: Directors and Producers
principle: Keep one director with clear final say over content
why: The director sets the game's direction, and multiple directors cause split opinions and unclear goals.
how: Name one director; if you divide the role, state explicitly who has the final say on what.
anti_pattern: Shared directing with no clear decision-maker.
quote: Usually, a team has one director. That's because the role entails charting a game's path, and you don't want split opinions or unclear goals.

title: Directors and Producers
principle: Let the director come up with the game's concept
why: Designing a concept is difficult without a grasp of the game's core appeal, which the director needs to hold.
how: Have the director originate the concept, even if a game designer later fleshes out the design.
anti_pattern: Separating the concept from the person who charts the game's path.

title: Directors and Producers
principle: Give producers budget, staffing and publicity so directors can focus
why: Producers weigh dev costs against projected sales and handle marketing, because a good game doesn't matter if nobody knows about it, while directors are very busy.
how: Assign a producer to financing, staffing and interviews, and build mutual trust so the director-producer split doesn't become a standoff.
example: Sakurai often takes on a producer's role himself, since Smash fighter reveal movies are marketing.

title: Establishing Characters Through Their Design
principle: Make sure everyone on a character understands its core essence
why: Matching a source design isn't enough; the people assigned need to understand the essence and draw it out further, which takes the whole team.
how: Write a short statement of each character's essence, share it with the team, and blend classic and newer design details when adapting.
anti_pattern: Copying a reference design literally but missing what makes the character feel like themselves.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate's Mii Fighter Nakoruru costume matched KOF XIV but felt off until it was revised.

title: Elementary School Play Testers
principle: Watch children play your build instead of asking them questions
why: Children, unlike jaded adults, always react honestly, revealing difficulties with the controls and what bores them.
how: With permission, invite staff members' kids and their friends, stand back, and note where they struggle or lose interest.
anti_pattern: Asking them directly what they think.
example: A child playing the original Smash Bros. shouted at how far a Falcon Punch knocked someone back.
quote: Rather than asking them directly, I would stand back and just try and see how they responded to the game.

title: Elementary School Play Testers
principle: Make playtests feel like a fun session with friends
why: Snacks and friends make it feel less like play testing and more like a fun gaming session, so reactions stay natural.
how: Let kids come in groups, provide snacks and keep the setting casual, after getting the permissions confidentiality and child well-being require.
quote: We'd prepare things like snacks, too, to help it to feel less like actual play testing and more like a fun gaming session with friends.

title: Elementary School Play Testers
principle: Use outside playtest reactions to keep the dev team motivated
why: The team was always happy to have these sessions, and during especially tough work they drive you forward.
how: Schedule kid playtests during hard stretches and let the team see or hear the reactions.
quote: When you're pushing through some especially tough work, stuff like this can really drive you forward.

title: Odds and Ends of Supervising: Sora Edition
principle: Give visual feedback and point out tiny flaws immediately
why: Small flaws are easy to overlook, and fine-tuning over and over is what raises quality.
how: Send retouched images, quick mouse sketches or a posed figure instead of words alone, and flag stray marks the moment you see them.
anti_pattern: Letting small flaws slide.
example: Sora's forward aerial posed with a figure; an extraneous mark on the Timeless River costume's face.
quote: These things are easy to overlook, so you should point them out as soon as you find them.

title: Give Yourself a Handicap When Balancing Your Game
principle: Use fresh testers from the start, and each one only once
why: Unfamiliar players are the best gauge, but they often lack time to finish and grow familiar, so the same person can't be called back a second or third time.
how: Rotate in new testers who start from the very beginning, treating each as a one-time first impression.
anti_pattern: Reusing the same outside tester as if they were still fresh.
quote: Naturally, the best solution is to ask someone who's unfamiliar with your game to come play it from the start

title: A Director’s Job is to Trim
principle: As director, trim the excess yourself when plans slip
why: It's faster when the director recognizes and addresses problems than when compromises come from producer-versus-director battles; finished products are the result of trimming and hard work.
how: When hardware limits, deadlines or workload go off plan, anticipate the damage, cut or offload the riskiest work, and reset the course.
anti_pattern: Leaving cuts to a fight between cost-focused producers and quality-focused directors.
example: Offloading "the heavy or flammable cargo" to get back on course.
quote: That's because a director not only creates, but is also responsible for trimming the excess.

title: A Director’s Job is to Trim
principle: Report trouble early with accurate information, even when struggling
why: Decisions built on incorrect premises are all wrong, and someone who admits at the last minute they can't finish loses the time an earlier fix could have saved.
how: Make it a rule to flag being stuck as soon as it happens, well before the deadline, with an honest status.
anti_pattern: Struggling silently and saying you can't do it at the deadline.
quote: And always give accurate information, even if you're having trouble!

title: A Director’s Job is to Trim
principle: Build cooperative relationships so work can be handed off quickly
why: If a struggling member comes to the director during the process, an appropriate solution can likely be found before time is lost.
how: Treat early reports as baton passes: reassign, re-scope or change approach right away.
quote: Within a team, it's best to build a cooperative relationship where you can quickly pass the baton.

title: Mr. Iwata
principle: Trust creators with content, but step in when problems arise
why: Iwata never told Sakurai how to approach his games' content, yet jumped in personally to help teams whenever problems came up.
how: Let directors own creative decisions; when a team is stuck, get hands-on to fix the issue rather than dictating content.
example: Iwata at HAL Laboratory, and later debugging Melee as head of Nintendo's corporate planning division.
quote: Personally speaking, he never told me how I should approach the content of my games.

title: Mr. Iwata
principle: Meet problems with calm analysis instead of anger
why: Iwata used logic rather than instinct, and where most people would lose their temper he stayed calm and offered analysis or suggestions.
how: When something goes wrong, analyze the cause and propose a fix before reacting emotionally.
anti_pattern: Losing your temper or taking offense.
quote: In situations where most people would lose their temper or get offended, he would remain calm and offer analysis or suggestions instead.

title: Mr. Iwata
principle: Make time for one-on-one conversations with team members
why: Iwata valued communication and found one-on-ones with employees incredibly effective, and wrote his own invitations despite his workload.
how: Schedule regular one-on-ones and send important invitations personally rather than through an assistant.
example: Iwata's one-on-ones from his HAL presidency onward.
quote: he'd make time to talk with his employees one-on-one— something I believe he felt to be incredibly effective.

title: Up is Down, and Down is Up
principle: Treat directions to your team as requests, not orders
why: People with ideas are powerless without others; instructions travel downstream, but the director is really asking the people who do the work, just as a publisher can't make customers buy.
how: Phrase direction as requests to the people doing the work, and never bark orders.
anti_pattern: Barking orders because you're the director or producer.
example: Customer and publisher: the customer is downstream in distribution but upstream in choosing the game.
quote: But in actuality, they're making requests from the bottom up to the dev team members who'll be doing the actual work.

title: Up is Down, and Down is Up
principle: Show every teammate respect regardless of rank or seniority
why: Nobody likes a demanding customer, so acting superior breeds resentment; everyone on the team is an ally working toward a better product.
how: Address all team members politely in name and tone, including new hires much younger than you, and treat disagreements as normal between allies.
anti_pattern: Acting superior or subservient; addressing new coworkers casually.
quote: Neither the director nor their team members should act superior or subservient to anyone else, I'd say.

title: Masahiro Sakurai on Creating Games: Finale Special
principle: Clear every review the same day, with a delivery cutoff
why: Putting reviews off invites trouble, and late-night deliveries around 11 PM were wrecking his sleep.
how: Require collaborators to deliver anything for same-day review by a fixed time (his was 8 PM), and send feedback as bullet points.
anti_pattern: Letting review requests spill into the next day.
example: HIKE's video and thumbnail deliveries, each episode getting about six to eight rounds of feedback.
quote: Putting them off is just asking for trouble.
